content.thinking:
I'm sketching the overall design: a wooden plinth base with a vertical eucalyptus trunk, and a koala built from voxel-style boxes gripping the branch.

I'll settle on a concrete layout: a wooden plinth base, a vertical trunk with a Y-fork, and a horizontal branch where the koala sits with its rump on the branch and back leaning against the trunk, forelimbs gripping a second angled branch in front.

Working out real-world proportions: a koala sitting upright is roughly 0.6-0.7m tall, so I'm setting the seat height around y=0.48 with the head topping out near 1.05, and the trunk standing about 1.3 tall. I'm placing the plinth, curving the vertical trunk with bark texturing, and adding a horizontal branch extending forward from the trunk for the koala to sit in.

I'm also adding a second upward branch with eucalyptus leaves, and thinking through pose logic -- maybe the koala sits on the branch facing a second trunk section directly in front and hugs it with its arms, which feels like a classic koala pose.

Actually that blocks the face from view, so I'm reconsidering: put the main trunk behind the koala at a slight offset, with a sturdy horizontal limb running sideways as the seat, and have the koala sit straddling that branch with legs resting forward.

Working out the koala's pose in detail: legs bent with feet clasping the branch near the buttocks, and arms reaching forward and up to hug a second, thinner cross branch at chest height in front of it.

I should add eucalyptus leaves clustered on the top fork and branch ends, using narrow elongated blue-green pixel-textured cards. For the koala itself, I'll build it chunky and voxel-ish mostly from boxes with some cellPaint sweeps for rounded tubes, keeping that hard-edged pixel texel look consistent across all surfaces.

Setting up the skeleton now: hips root, spine chain up through chest, neck, head with separate upper/lower jaw, ears, arms down to finger digits, legs down to toes, and no tail since koalas are vestigial there. Each bone gets a rigid box riding it, positioned and aimed to match the bone's orientation, keeping things simple by relying on world-axis alignment rather than fiddly roll corrections for most parts.

I'm planning a helper function that builds a tiled box segment between two joints, sized by width and depth, oriented along the direction from one joint to the next. For the look, I'm going with a textured fur palette -- grey body, cream belly, white fluffy ear interiors, a big black leathery nose, and small eyes -- rendered with dithered cell-paint shading.

Now I'm deciding how to apply the fur: cell-painted dithering for most of the body with texture tiles reserved for special features like the face and ears, settling on a texel size around 2cm so a roughly 1-meter-tall koala comes out to about 50 pixels high, with the head needing finer resolution.

I'm working through the dimensions more carefully -- using a finer texel of 0.0125m for the head and body details, which keeps the paint resolution reasonable (around 27x40 px for the torso) while reserving a coarser 0.02m texel for the stand's bark texture, since geometry size determines paint area regardless of detail level.

For the fur coloring, I'm designing a grey ramp with lighter and darker tones, then adding noise and streak grain so the fur reads naturally, with brightness varying by vertical position and belly/chest areas rendered lighter to create the characteristic koala coloring pattern.

Now I'm working out the plinth geometry—thinking of it as a cut log slice, possibly lathed with octagonal segments to keep the pixel texturing clean, positioned at the base to support the pose.

For the trunk, I'm placing a vertical post offset slightly back, running from near the base up to about shoulder height, and giving it an eight-sided sweep so I can paint eucalyptus bark texture: pale smooth bark with peeling vertical strips in orange, cream, and grey tones.

I also need to think about rigging—the model requires exactly one root joint, so I'm considering placing a "stand" root joint at the base, with a "hips" joint as its child, following the convention that hips or pelvis typically serve as the root or first joint in the spine chain.

Now I'm working out the koala's sitting posture against the trunk, defining the branch and body heights in model space—figuring out where the seat branch sits and where the koala's rump should rest on it.

I'm sketching the body proportions: pear-shaped torso leaning back against the trunk, with hips, chest, neck base and head center positioned along a slightly curved spine. Sitting height from branch to crown is around 0.6m, and I'm sizing the broad, round head to account for the koala's oversized furry ears.

I'm working out exact box dimensions for the stylized head, nose, ears and torso, slightly exaggerating proportions for the cartoon pixel look, with ears rendered as stepped fluffy disks and the torso/hips widened for the characteristic rump.

Now I'm mapping the full body height: seat around 0.48, rump bottom 0.50, hips center 0.62, chest 0.82, shoulders 0.92, head center 1.03, ears topping out near 1.17, with the overall model peaking around 1.5 including trunk and leaves — checking this against real koala proportions (0.6-0.85m body, ~0.5-0.6m sitting height) and it lines up well. I'm also placing the tree trunk behind the koala at a set depth and radius.

Now I'm checking the gap between the koala's back and the trunk surface, adjusting the trunk position slightly so the koala leans naturally against it with just enough contact. I'm also laying out a seat branch extending forward from the trunk with a slight rise, then working out the koala's sitting leg pose: hip joints positioned out to the sides, thighs angling forward and up toward the belly, and shins curving back down so the feet can grip the branch underneath.

Simplifying the foot placement, I'm settling on resting the feet along the branch with toes pointing forward, flanking the branch on either side rather than trying to wrap them precisely around it.

Since both feet can't fully sit atop the narrow branch, I'll flank it instead — positioning the feet at x=±0.07, y=0.47, with toes curling underneath and spreading so the inner toe pads wrap around the branch's sides, fitting the blocky puppet style.

I'm planning each foot as five small toe digits, grouping them into a hallux plus paired digits for a simplified joint chain, and placing the ankle points at roughly (±0.085, 0.515, 0.17) with toes extending forward toward where the branch passes through the feet's z-range.

Now I'm working out the arms, placing shoulders around (±0.17, 0.92, 0.02) and elbows near (±0.2, 0.78, 0.12), with hands gripping a forward branch -- but I realize that branch would need to pass through the torso, which occupies the chest region, so I need to reconsider how it connects to the trunk without intersecting the koala's body.

I'm reconsidering the branch geometry: maybe the forward support comes from a side fork off the trunk, or the trunk itself is Y-shaped and bends forward from one side, or the arrangement flips so the main trunk sits in front of the koala with a seat branch extending backward to support it.

I could go symmetric instead: a horizontal branch crossing in front of the chest, held up by a two-pronged fork, with both arms draped evenly over it for a balanced resting pose.

A second lower horizontal perch could let the koala sit with its rump supported while its arms grip the upper bar, making the whole thing read like a eucalyptus perch frame rather than something lopsided.

I'm picturing a sturdy vertical trunk behind the koala that forks near the top into two limbs curving forward around its sides, plus trying a simpler version with just a trunk and a separate horizontal crossbar bough for support.

Actually, a more natural pose: the koala sits gripping a seat branch directly with both hands and feet on either side, like sitting on a bench edge, with the trunk behind supporting its back. Above that, the trunk forks upward into two leafy limbs with eucalyptus foliage.

I extend the seat branch forward beyond the feet into a small leafy twig for visual interest near the head, then start working out the arm joint positions—shoulder, elbow, and wrist coordinates—checking the segment distances make anatomical sense.

Now I'm positioning the hands so they grip over the top of the branch, placing them side by side with fingers wrapping down either side, figuring out the box dimensions for palms and the opposable thumb digits.

Still positioning paw digits...

Let me tally up the full joint budget: root, hips, spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, arms, legs, and digit chains all add up to roughly 70 joints total, comfortably under the 160 limit. Now I'm working out foot placement on the seat, with toes wrapping around the sides at the right x and z coordinates.

I'm refining foot pad sizing and position so the sole rests partly on the branch top with toes curling down the outer edges, matching how the hands grip similarly. I'm adjusting the branch radius to around 0.05 for a realistic eucalyptus diameter, then checking how the koala's rump and hips sit straddling the branch top.

Now I'm working out leg geometry—hip, knee, and ankle coordinates with thigh and shin segment lengths—deciding to use a limb IK approach with bend direction hints rather than placing points manually, plus adding joint shapes at the knee for visual continuity.

For the body, I'm plotting the spine chain from hips through two spine segments up to the chest, then the neck leading to a head joint, and figuring out where the head box should be centered relative to that joint.

I'm now stacking the torso as separate hip, belly, and chest boxes with slightly varying widths and heights, keeping them centered along the vertical axis with small offsets to mimic a stepped pixel-art silhouette rather than a smooth loft.

For the voxel koala look, I'll stagger widths (rump widest, tapering up to shoulders) plus add rear thigh bulges for volume, then move on to blocking out a wide, rounded head box sized relative to the pixel grid.

The head gets small dark eye pixels placed asymmetrically, a separate darker nose box with highlight texture, a lighter muzzle box beneath it, and distinct upper/lower jaw boxes to give the face some structure rather than a flat blob.

I'll settle on a 3x3 pixel eye at 0.01 scale, which feels right for chunky pixel-art proportions without being too fine. For face coloring, I'm thinking grey cranium, slightly lighter grey-beige muzzle, and lighter cheeks to add some dimension.

Now I'm working out the ears: big round shapes extruded as stepped circles with roughly 0.10 diameter, using a helper function to generate the half-widths for each row to approximate the circle. I'm planning thinner fluff detailing inside each ear—a lighter cream center with a white fur rim—painted onto the extruded cells for texture.

Ears attach to the head via hinge joints (earL, earR), and I'm leaning toward using cellPaint for fur dithering across most boxes while reserving the more detailed skinBox texture technique specifically for the head where facial features need finer control.

Thinking through texel alignment, I'm treating paint cells and tile texels as equal-sized grids so mixed techniques stay visually consistent. For foliage, I'm planning eucalyptus leaves as slender sickle-shaped pixel sprites in blue-green-grey tones with a lighter center vein, plus a rounder juvenile leaf variant for variety.

I'm sizing leaves to match real-world eucalyptus proportions at the same pixel texel scale — landing on roughly 4x14 pixel leaves at 0.05x0.175 world units so they stay true to the 0.0125 texel grid rather than looking oversized. Now I'm thinking about how these leaves attach to the thin twig sweeps.

For positioning the leaves, I need frames that make them droop downward like real eucalyptus foliage rather than aligning straight along the twig's tangent — so I'll build manual frames at each leaf point oriented outward and down instead of using the default along-path facing.

To fix the edge-on vanishing problem, I should randomize flow per leaf so each one rotates horizontally in a different direction, then add bend to curve them downward along that flow.

With flow pointing down, the card face ends up horizontal, like a leaf blade lying flat and drooping — that's the look I want. I'll vary flow with some side randomness for tilt diversity, planning for roughly 120-200 leaf cards total, each simple geometry, enough for a eucalyptus-like hanging effect.

For the trunk bark, I'm setting up a cell-paint scheme mixing pale cream, dark peeling ribbons, and orange-salmon patches, using layered noise sampled along vertical axes to create natural streaking, plus adding knots and thin extruded bark-peel slabs leaning off the trunk surface for texture.

I'm also planning around 25 curling bark strips with cream undersides, dark eye-shaped knot holes, and a few green moss patches for added kitsch detail. For the base, I'm considering a log-slice plinth built as a lathed octagonal disc with pixel-ring painting, working out the stepped radius and extrusion profile needed to get a convincing round slab shape at the right scale.

Now I'm figuring out the growth rings by computing radial distance from the stand's center and quantizing it into alternating wood-tone bands, with bark-colored dithering on the side walls. I'm stacking a darker, wider lower disc with a narrower upper slice to form a two-tier plinth, then placing the trunk on top so the whole model's lowest point sits at ground level.

For base dressing, I'm scattering small gray stones, grass tufts, fallen leaf cards, and eucalyptus gumnuts (tiny cup-shaped clusters on twigs) around the plinth, skipping any text signage. For the koala itself, I'm adding fur dithering with random darker specks, white cheek tufts as stepped zigzag extrusions below the ears, a white chin, and starting on a white chest patch.

Now I'm detailing the rump with mottled brown/white spots, cream-dark claw tips, a highlighted black nose, a pale lower jaw with a dark mouth-line texture, and large ears, while skipping a tail, pouch, and whiskers since koalas lack prominent ones. I'm setting up a shared coat paint function that handles fur coloring consistently across all body parts.

Writing fur color ramp...

Still writing fur shading logic...

Trunk, branches, and plinth together add up to roughly 5.5 m² of painted surface, giving about 2.7mm per texel — plenty sharp relative to the 1.5-3cm paint texel target, so I'll stick with default atlas resolution rather than bumping to 2048.

Now I'm moving to the skeleton code, starting with a helper function that places a box segment between two points with given width, depth, color, and bone binding.

Finishing the segment helper and thinking through orientation — boxes aimed along the vector between points, limbs pointing downward work fine by default. Box UVs should work correctly with cell-paint snapping even on rotated faces, though slanted limb boxes will show slightly skewed cell patterns, which is acceptable.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, starting with a root joint at the floor and a spine chain parented to the hips.

Mapping out the spine chain's path points and names, then the neck chain, followed by a separate head joint (since the neck chain itself only needs one span) parented appropriately with its own role, and now starting work on the jaw joint.

For orientation I'm settling on using named local directions (forward/up/left/right) instead of raw vectors to keep things clearer, then setting up the arm chains with shoulder-elbow-wrist joints parented off the spine's chest tip since that's roughly at shoulder height.

I'm now working out finger joint counts per digit to keep the total skeleton joint budget under 160 -- considering 2 joints per digit across 20 digits (fingers plus toes) to stay efficient rather than 3.

Computing finger joint coordinates relative to the branch radius and hand frame, I'm working through base, mid, and tip positions so the fingers wrap naturally around the branch edge rather than floating outside it.

Spacing the five digits evenly across the z-range for the fingers, then setting up digit box dimensions and orientation for each segment...

Now thinking through the feet similarly — toes spaced along z near the branch grip point, with sole and toe boxes oriented the same way as the hand digits.

I'm planning a generic gripper-building function usable for both hands and feet, parameterized by pad size, digit count, and joint position, then checking that wrist and ankle joint coordinates line up correctly with the arm/leg bones feeding into them.

I'm also double-checking that the hand/foot pad actually touches the branch surface rather than floating above it, since the branch is slightly curved — so I need to lower the pad's y-position a bit to make contact.

For the feet, I'm placing ankles further out, sizing the sole pads, and spacing five toes evenly along the branch length so they sit near the branch's narrowing end, leaving the final twig segment bare. Now I'm working out the leg joint positions from hip to knee to ankle, trying to get a natural bent-leg pose with reasonable shin length.

Working through arm joint positions from shoulder to elbow to wrist, keeping the upper arms thick and stylized like a koala's stocky forelimbs, with the forearm tapering to the wrist. I'm adjusting shoulder placement inward to align with the torso's outer surface so the arms attach cleanly without overlap, then starting to lay out the rump box center position along the torso's hip, spine, and chest bones.

Now I'm working through the torso's belly and chest box placements, trying to get the koala's hunched, forward-leaning posture right by checking how much the trunk's front and back surfaces overlap with the rump at different heights, and nudging the trunk's lean so the spine curves forward without too much fur clipping.

Then I'm tracing the trunk's path upward behind the head using a catmull-rom curve with varying radius, adding a slight S-curve sideways offset for naturalness, and forking off two branch limbs going up and outward to the left and right where leaves will attach.

I'm thinking about overall proportions—keeping the trunk taller than the koala but capping it around 1.5-1.7m—and now adding a seat branch extending forward from the trunk at mid-height with its own taper, plus considering how to cap the cut end with a small disc showing growth rings.

For the ring texture on that cut end, I realize I can detect it's a flat end cap by checking if the face normal points strongly along one axis, then paint concentric rings based on radial distance from the branch's center axis—essentially building a generic bark-painting function that applies ring patterns to any flat-capped end, whether it's the seat stub or the trunk top.

I also want to add a rustic stand structure: two diagonal wooden braces running from the plinth up to the trunk, with small bolt details, plus leaf clusters scattered across the fork limbs, trunk top, the seat branch's tip, and a little twig sprouting near the koala's head with leaves positioned like a snack beside its face.

I'll mirror that twig to the model's right side too, keeping it clear of the head and ears by placing it further out in x. For the twig geometry, I'm designing a eucalyptus-style twig function that sweeps bark along a path of oriented frames, then attaches leaf cards using a small pixel-art texture for an elongated lanceolate leaf shape.

I'm also planning round silvery juvenile leaves for some twigs, plus tiny brownish gumnut capsules clustered in groups along the branch.

For ground dressing, I'm scattering flat leaf-litter cards, pebbles, and grass tufts around the base, skipping any text plaque. For the koala's fur, I'm adding jagged stepped-extrude tufts in white along the cheeks and chest to give it that spiky pixel-fur look.

I'm now scattering fur-tuft cards across the torso and jaw using a surface scatter function with distance filtering, sizing, and lean/flow parameters so the tufts drape downward over the body's stepped geometry, tinting the grey fur texture to match each part's base color.

I should preview and iterate, keeping triangle counts low—small boxes for digits and claws stay around 40 each. For head texture, I'm sizing the cranium in pixels and converting to world units, planning to dither fur shading across all faces using a bayer pattern tied to each face's color.

The front face gets eyes, lighter cheek zones, and a dark brow, while the top is darker near the ears. I'm adding a separate muzzle box sized in pixels, plus a protruding black leathery nose box positioned at the front-top of the muzzle, with lighter grey highlight pixels and two dark nostril pixels in its texture.

Now I'm setting up the skin layout dimensions for head, muzzle, jaw, and nose regions, planning to draw each as a uniform skinBox with fur texture layered using a Bayer dithering pattern for shading variation, then placing the eye pixels symmetrically across the head's front face.

I'm adding detail touches: a darker ring around each eye, lighter cheek patches, a darker forehead, and ear-base fluff, while positioning the muzzle box to protrude forward from the lower head with the nose on top and a pale stripe running down the nose bridge between the eyes.

Now I'm pinning down exact coordinates: the head joint sits forward at roughly (0, 0.99, 0.045), with the cranium centered around (0, 1.04, 0.07) so it spans from about y 0.965-1.115 and z -0.0175 to 0.1575, sitting directly on the shoulders with minimal neck. I'm placing the muzzle centered at (0, 1.0, 0.18) so it overlaps the cranium's front edge by about 0.015, keeping the proportions compact and koala-like.

Working out the nose, which protrudes slightly above and in front of the muzzle, and the jaw box positioned just below so it tucks under the muzzle with their edges meeting at y 0.969-0.9725. I'm planning to fake the mouth slit with a dark shaded row where the muzzle's bottom face meets the jaw's top face, rather than modeling an actual gap.

Now I'm positioning the ears at the top-sides of the head, computing the outward tilt and orientation vectors needed so each ear's extruded disc faces forward-outward correctly using a cross product to get the thickness axis.

For painting the ears, I'll use front face (n.z>0.3) for the cream inner ear with a white fringe ring, back face (n.z<-0.3) for grey fur dither, and walls for fur texture, measuring distance from the outline's origin to create the ring effect.

Defining ear outline shape...

Maybe skip tuft cards and keep it simpler, scattering a few fur accents directly on the ear surface instead. For the hands, I'll add small cream-dark claw boxes attached at each fingertip joint.

Now I'm writing a helper function to build box segments between two points, computing length and direction automatically from the joint positions so each bone box aligns correctly along its limb axis.

input.command: grep -n "^export" src/builder.ts | head -60; ls samples scratch 2>/dev/null | head; grep -n "koala" -ri samples -l | head
